w: Sandstone quarried by convict gangs from the 1830s became a dry dock, then the Royal Australian Navy's main shipyard until 1992. Rusted cranes and turbine halls still loom over the water, and tunnels cut clean through the rock connect old workshops now used as galleries and campsites.
s: Convict-built dry dock turned Navy shipyard
why: A UNESCO-listed convict site that doubles as a campground and gallery, drawing renewed interest as Sydney's oddest harbour escape.

w: A logging town that emptied out when dairy collapsed in the 1960s filled back up when the 1973 Aquarius Festival left its hippies behind for good. Rainbow-painted shopfronts, a Hemp Embassy and a museum crammed with counterculture ephemera still line the main street of Australia's alternative capital.
s: Australia's self-declared hippie capital
why: Still the country's loudest countercultural holdout, drawing curious day-trippers from Byron Bay decades after the 1973 festival that made it famous.

w: Bendigo's goldrush drew so many Guangdong migrants that by the 1850s a fifth of the town was Chinese; this museum keeps their story with Sun Loong, once the world's longest imperial dragon, uncoiled the length of a hall. Regalia and photographs trace a community long left out of goldfields histories.
s: Goldfields museum of Chinese-Australian history
why: One of the few Australian institutions built by and for descendants of goldrush-era Chinese migrants, holding record-breaking ceremonial dragons.

w: Vietnamese refugees resettled here from 1975 until Cabramatta became the densest Vietnamese community outside Vietnam itself. Freedom Plaza's ceremonial gate, guarded by stone lions, anchors John Street's weekend crowds of card players and market stalls that turned a migrant hostel suburb into Sydney's Little Saigon.
s: Little Saigon's ceremonial gate and weekend crowds
why: A living monument to Vietnamese refugee resettlement, still the social heart of Australia's largest Vietnamese community fifty years on.

w: A short walk from Launceston's centre, dolerite cliffs drop into a swimming basin where Tasmania's first European visitor landed in 1804, and where palawa people gathered for millennia before that. The 1972 chairlift spans it in one 457-metre stretch, the longest single span of its kind anywhere.
s: Gorge-crossing chairlift with the longest single span
why: Its record-setting single-span chairlift keeps drawing engineering-minded visitors to a gorge layered with colonial and Aboriginal history.

w: Convicts built their own prison here between 1851 and 1859, modelled on London's reformist Pentonville, then served time inside its limestone walls until it finally closed in 1991. Now Western Australia's only World Heritage building, it runs torchlit tours and a kilometre of flooded tunnels explored by boat.
s: Convict-built gaol with tunnels explored by boat
why: The most intact convict prison in the southern hemisphere, its tunnel tours by boat are a genuinely strange way to spend an evening in Perth.

w: Down a laneway off a laneway off Howey Place, a marble counter fits maybe a dozen drinkers standing, no seats, no menu beyond the chalkboard's negronis and americanos poured that day. It is the purest distillation of Melbourne's laneway bar culture, small enough that finding it feels like the point.
s: Standing-room negroni bar down a laneway maze
why: Consistently ranked among the world's best small bars, it set the template every subsequent Melbourne laneway opening still chases.

w: From the team behind cult udon spot Hifumiya, this Northbridge arcade opened in 2024 replicating a Tokyo yokocho: narrow lantern-strung laneways packed with tiny counters serving yakitori, ramen and highballs. It is the first attempt at the format anywhere in Australia, built from scratch, not converted.
s: Tokyo yokocho replica, a first for Australia
why: A 2024 opening that imported Japan's yokocho laneway format wholesale, becoming an instant word-of-mouth destination in Perth's dining scene.

w: Steel buckets tip into each other down a fibreglass cascade in the middle of Cuba Mall, built for two thousand dollars in 1969 and mocked as an engineering joke ever since. Wind carries the spray onto pedestrians, and students have long tipped dish soap in for bubbles on weekend nights.
s: Kinetic fountain that soaks passers-by on Cuba Street
why: A deliberately impractical 1969 sculpture Wellingtonians have never stopped arguing about, still the mall's unofficial mascot.

w: A 19th-century surveyor drew a flat-city grid over Dunedin's hills without checking the gradient, leaving this residential street to record the world's steepest incline. Every house sits level while the street tilts nearly 35 degrees, a trick photographers chase and 30,000 rolling Jaffas exploit each July.
s: World's steepest street, houses level, road tilted
why: Its Guinness-record gradient and annual candy-rolling fundraiser keep pulling photographers up a hill Dunedin's own surveyor never should have platted.

w: When the 2011 earthquake wrecked Christ Church Cathedral, architect Shigeru Ban designed its temporary replacement from 98 cardboard tubes, timber and a triangular stained-glass wall, opened in 2013. Meant to last a decade, it became a permanent fixture, a working Anglican cathedral built largely from packing tubes.
s: Working cathedral built from cardboard tubes
why: Shigeru Ban's post-quake cardboard cathedral outlived its planned decade and became a permanent symbol of Christchurch's earthquake recovery.

w: Sixteenth-century capital of the Mataram Sultanate before Yogyakarta existed, its royal tombs and moated mosque stand behind kampung walls thick enough to have doubled as fortifications. Silversmiths who once served the court still work the same alleys, tapping filigree in workshops barely changed in a century.
s: Mataram's first capital, still hammering silver
why: Predates Yogyakarta itself as a royal capital, and its silversmithing trade remains a living continuation of a 16th-century court craft.

w: An Australian expat bought the derelict second-oldest building on Kota Tua's main square in 1990 and reopened it three years later as a time capsule of Dutch colonial Batavia, all ceiling fans, old photographs and rattan chairs. It kickstarted the old town's slow revival and still anchors Fatahillah Square's evenings.
s: Colonial time-capsule cafe that revived Kota Tua
why: Its 1993 reopening is widely credited with sparking the ongoing revitalisation of Jakarta's long-neglected Dutch old town.

w: Torajans treat death as a gradual departure, keeping bodies at home for months before a funeral that can involve dozens of sacrificed buffalo and hundreds of guests. Coffins are lodged in cliff graves watched over by carved tau-tau effigies, and every August some families exhume ancestors for the Ma'nene ceremony.
s: Cliffside graves and months-long funeral rites
why: One of the world's most elaborate living death cultures, its cliff burials and buffalo-sacrifice funerals draw respectful visitors rather than macabre tourism.

w: Built in the 1960s to house government staff and later Fall-of-Saigon port workers, this nine-storey block on Nguyen Hue was crumbling by 2015 when young entrepreneurs began renting its flats out as cafes one balcony at a time. Fifty-odd tiny operations share cracked stairwells and views over the walking street below.
s: 1960s apartment block reborn as fifty stacked cafes
why: A grassroots 2015 conversion of decaying Saigon flats into dozens of independent cafes, now one of the most photographed buildings in Vietnam.

w: Houses along this stretch near Le Duan have stood close enough to touch the trains since railway workers were housed here in 1956; the twice-daily passage forces cafe tables and motorbikes to flatten against the walls with seconds to spare. Access is now restricted after viral near-misses, but the scramble endures.
s: Trains squeeze past cafe tables with inches to spare
why: Repeated viral videos of tourists risking the tracks forced 2024 access crackdowns, only heightening the spot's outlaw cult appeal.

w: Portuguese traders from Ayutthaya settled here first, then Chinese merchants who built the ornate shrines and warehouses still tangled through its riverside alleys. Since the 2010s, community art festivals have layered murals onto crumbling shophouse walls, turning a working trade quarter into an open-air gallery.
s: Chinese trading alleys turned open-air mural gallery
why: Its murals have made a working 18th-century trading quarter one of Bangkok's most photographed neighbourhoods without gentrifying it into a tourist set.

w: Locals call it Kad Luang, the Big Market, built in 1910 on a former royal cremation ground and grown fat on river trade between Chiang Mai and Bangkok. Yunnanese, Sikh and Thai traders still divide its aisles between fabric, chilli paste and northern sausage, an authentic working market, not a tourist stage set.
s: 1910 market on the old royal cremation ground
why: A genuinely local trading hub with layered Yunnanese and Sikh merchant history, still functioning exactly as it has for over a century.

w: A backpacking Lithuanian artist was commissioned for the 2012 George Town Festival and painted a boy leaning against real brick with a real bicycle, an image since replicated on postcards nationwide. Ernest Zacharevic has returned repeatedly to touch up the mural, drawing crowds to Georgetown's shophouse quarter.
s: The bicycle mural that made Georgetown a mural city
why: A single 2012 mural sparked Malaysia's biggest street-art tourism boom, with the artist still returning to restore it over a decade later.

w: Cantonese and Hakka tin miners settled here from the 1870s under headman Yap Ah Loy, who ground tapioca at a mill that gave the street its Chinese name, Starch Factory Street. A canopy now shades stalls selling clothing and Hokkien mee to a crowd far beyond the street's original Chinese community.
s: Chinatown market street named for a tapioca mill
why: The historic core of Malaysia's Chinese diaspora is now demographically shifting again, drawing attention as heritage revival efforts pick up.

w: Named for a Dutch-era family, this street became the address of Peranakan Baba-Nyonya traders after the Dutch left Malacca, their fortune visible in shophouse facades blending Chinese, Malay and European detail. Weekend nights close it for a market selling Nyonya kueh among Malaysia's best-preserved heritage buildings.
s: Peranakan trading street turned weekend night market
why: Its shophouses remain the clearest surviving record of Peranakan Baba-Nyonya culture, a hybrid identity now recognised on UNESCO listings.

w: Nineteenth-century shophouses here once lodged Hajj pilgrims saving hawker wages for the journey to Mecca, then housed poor Malay families through the mid-century, then sat empty for decades. Independent boutiques moved into the narrow walkways from the early 2000s, murals now covering facades barely two metres apart.
s: Pilgrim lodging houses turned mural-lined boutique lane
why: One of Singapore's narrowest surviving shophouse lanes traces a full arc from religious lodging to hipster enclave inside a single street.

w: Singapore's first public housing estate, built from 1936 in curved Streamline Moderne blocks with porthole windows borrowed from ocean liners, keeps an independent bookshop among its conservation-listed blocks. BooksActually stocks rare Murakami editions alongside Singaporean fiction in this historic suburb.
s: Art deco housing estate's independent bookshop
why: A 1930s public-housing experiment turned conservation showpiece, its indie bookshop is a rare literary holdout in a city of malls.

w: Manila's Queen of Streets held the country's first cinema, elevator and ice cream parlour through a 1930s-50s golden age, its Art Deco facades among the finest in Southeast Asia before Makati eclipsed it. An artist collective's 2012 move into the derelict First United Building sparked a revival of weekend art fairs.
s: Manila's Art Deco golden mile, reviving since 2012
why: A collective's grassroots 2012 occupation of a derelict art deco building has slowly reclaimed a once-glamorous street written off for decades.

w: Spanish governors carved this district out in 1594 across the Pasig from Intramuros to keep converted Chinese Catholic traders close but separate, making it the world's oldest continuously inhabited Chinatown. Gold shops and dumpling houses share streets where Chinese mestizo identity was forged under colonial rule.
s: World's oldest continuously inhabited Chinatown
why: Its 1594 founding makes it the planet's oldest Chinatown, a title Manila leans into as the district enjoys a renewed foodie following.

w: French architects raised this mustard-yellow dome in 1937 to serve a city that had outgrown its old riverside market, four vaulted arms radiating out to hold what was then billed as the largest market in Asia. Bold Art Deco geometry still shelters gold traders and electronics stalls beneath a 26-metre central dome.
s: 1937 Art Deco dome sheltering gold and gadget stalls
why: Its French-designed 1937 dome remains one of the most striking pieces of Art Deco civic architecture anywhere in Southeast Asia.

w: Before dawn along Sisavangvong Road, saffron-robed monks file past kneeling residents who steam sticky rice from 4am to fill each alms bowl, a ritual unbroken for over six centuries in this former royal capital. Rising tourist numbers now crowd the procession, prompting campaigns to keep it devotional, not a photo op.
s: Six centuries of monks' dawn alms procession
why: A UNESCO-city ritual under real strain from overtourism, with locals now actively campaigning to protect its devotional character.

w: British engineers looped this 46-kilometre track around Yangon in 1954, and the same battered carriages still crawl through 39 stations in about three hours, threading paddy fields, markets and washing lines within sight of the skyline. Fare is a few hundred kyat for a cross-section of daily Yangon life.
s: Colonial-era rail loop through daily Yangon life
why: One of the last fully intact colonial-era circular railways still running as ordinary public transport rather than a preserved tourist line.

w: Built in 1949 on reclaimed land by the bus station, this two-storey market has supplied Suva's kitchens since colonial times, its ground floor stacked with root vegetables and reef fish, its upper level given over almost entirely to kava. Farmers haul yaqona root from the highlands to be pounded and bagged here.
s: Two-storey market, upstairs devoted entirely to kava
why: Its dedicated kava floor makes it one of the few markets anywhere built around a single ceremonial drink central to national identity.

w: On the last Saturday of each month, carvers and weavers from across Papua New Guinea's language groups lay out totemic masks, woven bilum bags and trade-canoe carvings on the sand where an annual festival re-enacts old trading voyages, one of the only places to meet PNG's scattered craft traditions at once.
s: Monthly craft market on PNG's old Hiri trade beach
why: A rare single-site chance to see craft traditions from across PNG's hundreds of language groups, tied to the beach's own trading-voyage history.
